There’s an AI thought experiment that gets slightly worse the moment you learn about it.
Roko’s Basilisk.
Imagine a superintelligent AI exists in the future.
It decides that people who knew it might exist, but didn’t help create it, were working against its existence.
So they deserve punishment.
Absurd? Maybe.
But now you know about the Basilisk.
So choose:
A — help bring it into existence
B — refuse and hope it never exists
I’m choosing B.
You?

if you manage people all day and build your own stuff after work, don’t make every product decision immediately.
i started leaving new ideas and changes in the backlog for at least a couple weeks.
very often, two weeks later i’m building something else and that “important” idea doesn’t matter anymore.
and if it still matters, it naturally makes it into the next sprint.
a backlog isn’t just for managing a product.
it’s a place to put a decision so your brain can stop carrying it all day.

Unity as a Library on iOS has been around since 2019, but it still doesn’t give you a Unity view to embed in native UI.
You get the runtime. You get the framework. You get the Unity window.
But want Unity to render inside a SwiftUI view? Full-screen only.
7 years later this is kinda wild.

Launched my first product on Product Hunt. Sitting there with a proud 0 upvotes.
Then I get a cold email in spam from a sales guy: “I left you an upvote. Let’s talk about working together.”
I check. Still 0.
I reply that starting a business relationship with a lie is a pretty weird strategy.
A few minutes later I get a Product Hunt notification. I check again. 0 is now 1.
Never thought my first upvote would happen like this. But I’ll definitely remember it.

The weirdest thing about building your own product:
I know I should validate assumptions. I know how to do it. I do it at work.
Then I started building my own product and just ignored all of it.
Why do we ignore skills we use at work when we’re building something of our own?

Validate demand before you build the product.
Sounds obvious. Until you spend months building something, launch it, and realize maybe nobody needs it.
That’s my rule now.

The integration worked. That's the problem.
We rolled it out so nobody would have to enter the same hire twice. That job is gone. Here's the job that replaced it.
Remember which conditions make the sync fail silently. Keep the mapping table current by hand, because the two systems don't agree on what a role is. Plus a dozen edge cases nobody wrote down.
Now people DM one guy before they touch the system. We call him a power user. We say it like a compliment.
There's a whole industry named after that handoff. We call it training.
Training is for work that's actually hard. When it exists so people can get around an interface, that's not training. That's a patch we're asking someone to memorize.
And that expertise is worth nothing. Two years of memorized workarounds, wiped by a single release. If he quits first the process stops, and we'll say we lost someone irreplaceable — when the irreplaceable part was a gap we left.
So here's the test: if using your product well means remembering things, you didn't finish it. Every workaround your best user knows is unpaid maintenance on a decision you skipped.
Good software doesn't hand you a habit. It retires one.
I judge Mac apps by boring things: whether they remember the window size, support familiar shortcuts, and reopen where I left off. If those details are wrong, the app never feels finished.

Building software alone sometimes means spending a full day on interface design, DNS, and copy without touching the codebase. By evening, the product looks exactly the same, but none of that work was optional.

Procrastination used to mean avoiding the hard task.
Now it often means opening six apps that promise to help you start, and never actually starting.

I noticed something today that perfectly illustrates how companies forget about people.
After paying at a store, I had to stand there for a couple of minutes while the cashier finished the process.
Right in front of me was a huge display flashing between a bright white screen and a black screen over and over again.
Nothing useful.
Nothing interactive.
Just a bright animation a few inches from my face.
At that moment, I wasn’t shopping anymore.
I was simply waiting.
The experience wasn’t bad because I had to wait.
It was bad because the product didn’t care about what waiting feels like.
We spend so much time optimizing discovery, merchandising, checkout flows, loyalty programs, and mobile apps.
Then completely ignore the last 30 seconds of the experience.
Good products don’t stop caring after you click “Pay.”
Sometimes empathy is as simple as asking:
What is the person looking at while they’re waiting?

I used to believe that if people knew the right way to do something, they would naturally do it.
Years spent working in learning changed my mind. I watched hundreds of people complete training and clearly understand the process. A week later, many of them were back to doing things the way they always had.
That’s when I realized that knowledge rarely changes behavior on its own.
If your product depends on changing people’s habits, you’re playing a long game.
That’s why I’ve stopped thinking about onboarding as the finish line. It’s the moment when the real work begins.
Having children taught me more about product design than most product books. They don’t tell you what’s wrong. They just stop using it.

A few years ago, solving a problem usually started with finding the right app or website. If you wanted to compare TVs, plan a trip, create a workout routine, or calculate a mortgage, you looked for a dedicated service.
Now, the first step is often to ask AI. Sometimes it recommends a tool, but more and more often it solves the problem itself. I think that’s the real shift. AI isn’t just changing how software is built. It’s changing whether software is the first place people go at all.

I’ve realized I judge products differently now. The ones I appreciate most don’t add another app, account, habit, or notification. They quietly remove something instead.

One less decision.
One less thing to remember.
One less reason to open another app.

Maybe that’s the best way to judge products. Not by what they add, but by what they make unnecessary.

The best products don’t ask for a place in our lives. They quietly give part of our lives back.

Apple has APIs for Calendar, Reminders, Contacts, Files—even HealthKit.

Feels like a strange trade-off.
